questions.q: How does fail2ban detect a brute-force attempt in the first place?
options: It watches log files, like /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure, matching failed-login patterns with a per-service filter
It inspects raw network packets in real time as they arrive
It requires the protected application to call a fail2ban API directly
It only works if SELinux is also installed and enforcing
questions.explain: fail2ban doesn't inspect network traffic directly — it watches log files using regex-based filters that describe what a failed login looks like for a given service.

questions.q: What does fail2ban actually do once a source IP crosses the configured failure threshold?
options: It permanently deletes the user account that was targeted
It emails the attacker a warning
It inserts a firewall rule (iptables, nftables, or firewalld) that drops or rejects traffic from that IP for a set period
It shuts down the entire network interface
questions.explain: fail2ban acts by adding a firewall rule that blocks traffic from the offending IP for the jail's configured bantime.

questions.q: In a jail.local entry, what do maxretry, findtime, and bantime each control?
options: maxretry sets the firewall type, findtime sets the log path, and bantime sets the filter name
They are three different names for the exact same setting
maxretry is the number of failures that trigger a ban, findtime is the window those failures must occur in, and bantime is how long the resulting ban lasts
They only apply to the sshd jail and no other service
questions.explain: maxretry failures within findtime trigger a ban lasting bantime — for example, 5 failures in 10 minutes earning a 1-hour ban.

questions.q: What command immediately removes an active ban on a specific IP from the sshd jail?
options: sshd -t
auditctl -w 203.0.113.42
fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip 203.0.113.42
fail2ban-client status
questions.explain: fail2ban-client set <jail> unbanip <ip> lifts a ban immediately, useful if a legitimate user was caught by the threshold.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why does fail2ban still matter on an SSH server that already has PasswordAuthentication no set?
options: It provides defense in depth against future misconfiguration, protects other log-matchable services beyond SSH, and keeps connection-flood noise from accumulating in logs
fail2ban automatically disables itself once PasswordAuthentication no is detected
fail2ban only protects password-based logins and becomes inert once keys-only auth is enabled
It has no remaining value once password auth is disabled, since there's nothing left to brute-force
questions.explain: Even with keys-only SSH, fail2ban guards against a future misconfiguration, protects other services with matchable failure patterns, and limits the log noise and resource use from repeated failed attempts.
